name: Array Splitting
description: You are given an array $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ and an integer $$$k$$$. You are asked to divide this array into $$$k$$$ non-empty consecutive subarrays. Every element in the array should be included in exactly one subarray. Let $$$f(i)$$$ be the index of subarray the $$$i$$$-th element belongs to. Subarrays are numbered from left to right and from $$$1$$$ to $$$k$$$. Let the cost of division be equal to $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (a_i \cdot f(i))$$$. For example, if $$$a = [1, -2, -3, 4, -5, 6, -7]$$$ and we divide it into $$$3$$$ subbarays in the following way: $$$[1, -2, -3], [4, -5], [6, -7]$$$, then the cost of division is equal to $$$1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 2 - 5 \cdot 2 + 6 \cdot 3 - 7 \cdot 3 = -9$$$. Calculate the maximum cost you can obtain by dividing the array $$$a$$$ into $$$k$$$ non-empty consecutive subarrays.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ ($$$ |a_i| \le 10^6$$$).
output_specification: Print the maximum cost you can obtain by dividing the array $$$a$$$ into $$$k$$$ nonempty consecutive subarrays.
subsubtopic: 42. C++ STL Sort and Custom Comparator
approach_summary: Apply C++ STL Sort and Custom Comparator paradigm under the Basics framework. Exploit problem invariants to reduce state space and achieve optimal complexity.
